matches.rationale: The finding demonstrates with p‑values from Table A9 that the paper's broad claims of superiority (e.g. 14.6% improvement, outperforms all baselines) lack statistical support, which directly corresponds to the ground‑truth issue of missing variability/confidence intervals and overstatement in the abstract.
No finding mentions or identifies the fabricated "Filippini, 1892" reference; the findings discuss methodological inconsistencies and statistical support but not a fake citation.

No finding addresses the inconsistency about action embeddings being computed as a difference of state embeddings and how that difference is used in the loss/prediction heads; the findings focus on graph refinement and statistical claims.
No finding points out the missing hyperparameter tuning details for re‑implemented baselines; the available findings do not cover experimental design fairness in baseline optimization.

The finding uses significance testing to show that many of the reported superiority claims lack statistical significance, matching the ground‑truth concern that Table 1 shows only point estimates without variance or confidence intervals, thereby inflating confidence in the improvements.
No finding discusses missing ethical considerations, bias, or failure‑mode disclosure in the conclusion; the findings are about mathematical/statistical and setup issues.

No finding identifies the contradiction between computing cross‑entropy losses on all frames with ground‑truth labels (Section 3.1) and the later use of pseudo labels (Section 3.2); the closest finding is about frame‑level state labels for graph refinement, not loss computation.
No finding addresses the inflated rhetorical language ("powerful", "promising pathway") in the introduction; the findings are factual/methodological, not about tone or overhyped phrasing.
No finding mentions the suspiciously small performance change when increasing graph concepts from 5 to 15 (Table 4); the findings do not discuss Table 4 at all.

No finding captures the ambiguity regarding optional privileged information and whether it creates an unrealistic or leak‑prone evaluation protocol; the finding about SAGE relying on candidate entity names is a separate issue.
No finding discusses the disproportionate training times (8 hours for ChangeIt vs. 30 minutes for HowToChange); the findings do not cover training‑time anomalies.
No finding identifies the absence of criteria/validation for the VLM‑based frame filtering step; the finding about frame‑set F for graph refinement does not overlap with this filtering ambiguity.

No finding points out that the claimed generalization to multi‑action videos remains unevaluated; the only sensitivity to generalization claims is about statistical significance, not about scope of evaluation.

No finding addresses the overstated future‑work rhetoric in the conclusion claiming integration into foundation models and skill discovery; the findings are about technical inconsistencies and statistical support.
No finding discusses the unexplained large performance drops for LFC and VidOSC on novel objects/actions in Table 2(b); the findings are not about missing analysis of baseline degradation.
